report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: To identify EEG-derived markers of cortical excitability that best distinguish people with epilepsy from healthy controls while maintaining stability across repeated recordings, and to assess the influence of antiseizure medication (ASM) burden on these measures.

Scalp EEG recordings from the Temple University Hospital EEG Epilepsy Corpus were analyzed, including 1,404 recordings from 96 individuals with neurologist-confirmed epilepsy and 85 healthy controls across multiple sessions.

Eight global EEG measures were evaluated: aperiodic exponent and offset, sample entropy, detrended fluctuation analysis exponent and derived index, spatial gamma-band phase consistency, and absolute and relative alpha power.
Primary group inference used linear mixed-effects models to account for repeated recordings and sessions within participants.
Secondary analyses examined group differences in measures temporal stability and cross-metric correlation.
We examined only in epilepsy group associations between EEG-derived metrics and ASMs count, and their impact on cross-metric correlations.
In the mixed-effects models, aperiodic offset and exponent were the only measures with FDR-robust group effects.
Aperiodic offset showed higher consistency in epilepsy than in healthy controls (standardized epilepsy-minus-healthy beta = 0.52, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.78, FDR-adjusted p = 0.001).
Across sessions, consistency was higher in epilepsy for aperiodic offset exponent (beta = 0.32, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.54, FDR-adjusted p = 0.018).
Cross-metric correlation patterns were largely preserved between groups.
Medication associations were.
Epilepsy is a chronic disorder of brain excitability characterized by a persistent predisposition of neuronal networks to generate spontaneous, hypersynchronous discharges and seizures 1.

text.text: Cortical excitability refers to the responsiveness of cortical neurons to incoming input, and is shaped by the dynamic balance between excitatory and inhibitory (E/I) neurotransmission, intrinsic membrane properties, and network-level interactions 2 .

text.text: The central role of excitability in epilepsy is reflected in the mechanisms of antiseizure medications (ASMs).

Although ASMs act through diverse molecular targets-including enhancement of GABAergic inhibition, attenuation of glutamatergic transmission, modulation of voltagegated ion channels, and regulation of presynaptic neurotransmitter release-they converge on a common physiological effect: reducing pathological neuronal and network excitability, thereby limiting the emergence and propagation of epileptiform activity [3] [4] [5] [6].

text.text: Moreover, given the routine use of EEG in the diagnosis and longitudinal monitoring of epilepsy, multiple measures hold potential for translation into potential clinical applications, enabling the assessment of excitability-related changes using a widely available, non-invasive recording modality.

Candidate metrics include the aperiodic exponent and offset of the power spectral density, parameterized using FOOOF, which reflect the 1/f structure of neural activity and have been proposed as indirect markers of E/I balance 14, 15 .

text.text: Additional measures include sample entropy, which quantifies signal complexity 16, 17 , detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA), which characterizes long-range temporal correlations 18 ; spatial high-gamma phase consistency, reflecting large-scale network synchrony [19] [20] [21] , and alpha-band power, an established correlate of cortical inhibition 22 .

Within epilepsy, the medication list allows an exploratory analysis using a coarse count of recognized ASM names, but metadata from the public repository do not quantify dose, duration, or treatment effect.
We compared complementary resting-state EEG features that have been proposed as candidate proxies of cortical physiology relevant to excitability.
Specifically, we evaluate their group differences, temporal stability, and exploratory epilepsy-only associations with ASM count using a unified whole-brain analytical framework.

Ultimately, this work compares candidate EEG-derived measures of cortical excitability, examining their potential relevance for characterizing epilepsy and monitoring changes across repeated recordings.

text.text: Recordings were stored in European Data Format (EDF), and subjects could contribute multiple sessions acquired on different dates, enabling assessment of both between-subject differences and within-subject longitudinal stability.
Session-level metadata were extracted from the accompanying metadata file and linked to recordings using subject-session identifiers.

The TUEP dataset does not provide structured patient-level diagnosis labels identifying epilepsy type and anatomical lateralization, preventing more detailed analysis on epilepsy type or spatial location of the effects.
Medication names were parsed using a predefined dictionary of generic and brand antiseizure medications (ASMs), and the number of distinct ASMs prescribed at each recording was determined.
Dose, daily schedule, treatment duration, adherence and serum concentration were not available, preventing more detailed analyses beyond those based on the number of ASMs.
All EEG recordings were processed in MATLAB using EEGLAB 2024.2.1 43 and Brainstorm 44 .

text.text: Recordings were imported with pop_biosig, channel labels were standardized to the international 10-20 nomenclature, non-EEG channels and duplicate labels were removed, and electrode locations were assigned using the standard 10-05 template.
Segments corresponding to photic stimulation were automatically identified using stimulation channels and removed, including 10 s before the first pulse and 10 s after the last pulse.
Recordings with fewer than 2 min of remaining data were excluded.
Data sampled above 250 Hz were downsampled to 250 Hz, high-pass filtered at 1 Hz, and notch filtered between 59-61 Hz.
Artifact removal was performed in two stages to preserve continuous EEG segments, as several measures are sensitive to signal discontinuities.
An initial Artifact Subspace Reconstruction (ASR) pass was used only to generate a sample-level quality mask.
The longest continuous clean segment was retained and classified as PASS_GOLD (≥5 min), PASS_MIN (2-5 min), or FAIL (<2 min); accepted segments were truncated to a maximum duration of 10 min.

text.text: A second ASR pass was then applied to the selected segment using burst correction and Riemannian interpolation (ASR; clean_artifacts) 45 .

text.text: Independent component analysis (ICA) was performed using extended Infomax.
ICA weights were estimated on data downsampled to 100 Hz and transferred to the original sampling rate; principal component analysis was applied when necessary to compensate for rank deficiency.
Components were classified using ICLabel 46 , and those representing eye, muscle, or cardiac artifacts were removed using probability thresholds (>0.80 artifact, <0.15 brain).

All recordings underwent visual quality control based on their power spectra before being retained for analysis.

Group differences: For each measure, we fitted a linear mixed-effects model with group as a fixed effect and random intercepts for participant and for session nested within participant: measure ~ group + (1 | participant) + (1 | participant-session).
This accounts for repeated recordings per participant and for correlation among recordings from the same session.
Healthy participants were the reference group.
Models including age, and age and sex, were run as sensitivity analyses.
Temporal stability: Within-participant consistency was estimated separately in each group with nested variance-components models (measure ~ 1 + (1 | participant) + (1 | participant-session)).

From these we derived two intraclass correlations (ICC): same-session consistency (recordings from the same participant and session) and across-session consistency (recordings from the same participant in different sessions).
Group differences in ICC were tested with participant-level permutation, and confidence intervals were obtained by participant-level bootstrap.

Cross-measure structure: We compared the Spearman correlation matrices of the eight measures between healthy and epilepsy participants using a global permutation test on the difference between matrices, with individual pairs tested descriptively.
This was repeated at recording, session and participant level to check robustness to aggregation.
For each participant-session, ASM exposure was the number of distinct ASMs.

We split it into a within-person component (session count minus the participant's mean count) and a between-person component (participant mean count) and fitted, for each measure, session-mean measure ~ within-person ASM count + participant mean ASM count + (1 | participant).
The within-person coefficient estimates the change in a measure associated with one additional ASM relative to the participant's usual regimen.
The between-person coefficient is cross-sectional and may be confounded by indication, severity or clinical history.
For the analysis details see Supplementary Materials (S2 section).

In this study, we performed a systematic, large-scale evaluation of EEG-derived proxies of cortical excitability in epilepsy, leveraging the longitudinal structure of the Epilepsy Corpus EEG open database.

By comparing multiple candidate metrics within a unified analytical framework, we sought to determine their: i) performance in terms of group (epilepsy vs healthy) differences; ii) temporal stability; iii) cross-metric consistency and iv) examine the influence of medication within the epilepsy group.
Several key findings emerged from this analysis.
Aperiodic spectral parameters (offset and exponent) were the only EEG-derived metric showing group differences after correction for multiple comparisons in the mixed-effect models.
Specifically, patients displayed a larger aperiodic offset and exponent values as compared to controls.
The higher aperiodic exponent and offset in epilepsy agree with previous scalp and intracranial work, including our own, in focal epilepsy 3, 23, 52 .

text.text: Within the E/I framework, a steeper spectral slope is usually read as relatively stronger inhibition 14, 15.

text.text: However, this interpretation is consistent with previous work from our group and others showing increased inhibitory tone during the interictal and peri-ictal periods 3, 23, 24, 53 .

text.text: In this context, the findings align with the interictal suppression hypothesis, according to which epileptic networks recruit inhibitory processes during the interictal state to constrain pathological synchronization and reduce seizure likelihood.
Under this view, the elevated aperiodic exponent may reflect a relatively stable background state of compensatory regulation that coexists with an underlying susceptibility to seizure generation.
Other studies on invasive recordings do not confirm the findings above, but still advocate for aperiodic properties to be considered excitation / inhibition markers, and to fluctuate overtime 52 .

text.text: While findings in focal epilepsy (including TLE) consistently show higher exponent suggesting inhibitory compensation, studies of generalized epilepsy have found the opposite, lower exponent consistent with hyperexcitability 54 .

text.text: The composition of the current cohort may account for this directionality.

Additionally, the persistence of these effects after averaging across subjects suggests that aperiodic parameters reflect a relatively trait-like property of epileptic networks rather than transient state fluctuations 26, 35 .
text.formatted: Additionally, the persistence of these effects after averaging across subjects suggests that aperiodic parameters reflect a relatively trait-like property of epileptic networks rather than transient state fluctuations <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">35</ref> .

text.text: Because the database has no structured syndrome or lateralization labels, we could not test whether the direction of the effect depends on epilepsy type.
A heterogeneous, probably focal-dominated cohort may therefore explain the direction we observed.
Two caveats limit how far these findings can be interpreted.
First, the exponent effect was less robust than the offset effect.
It met the FDR threshold in the group-only model but not after adjusting for age, with or without sex, although its direction and magnitude were similar.
The offset effect held in all three specifications.
We therefore consider the offset the more reliable group marker here and the exponent a consistent but more tentative one.
Second, the aperiodic exponent and offset are correlated descriptors of the same spectral fit.
Broadband offset is sensitive to overall signal amplitude, which can be influenced by non-neural factors such as skull and scalp properties.
The remaining six measures did not show a group difference after correction.
Their sensitivity to epilepsy in this dataset is therefore not supported, and we cannot rule out smaller effects that this global, heterogeneous routine-EEG approach was not able to detect.
In epilepsy, aperiodic offset and exponent were reproducible across sessions acquired on different days, whereas in healthy controls they were essentially not reproducible (ICC ≈ 0).
We interpret this as a difference in between-subject variance.
In healthy adults the aperiodic spectrum varies little between people compared with its fluctuations with vigilance, arousal and recording conditions, so the ICC is low.
In epilepsy, patients differ markedly in etiology, network involvement and treatment, and these differences appear to be expressed in a lasting individual spectral profile.

This fits the view that elevated aperiodic offset and exponent reflect a chronic, trait-like property of epileptic networks (for example a persistent compensatory inhibitory tone) rather than a transient interictal state, and it links the two main findings of the study.
Alpha power followed a different pattern.
Absolute alpha was highly consistent within a session in epilepsy (ICC 0.87) but not across sessions.
Alpha is strongly modulated by vigilance, drowsiness, eye state and attention, which are largely constant within a recording but differ between visits, as this pattern would predict.
Together, these results suggest that different measures may serve different purposes.

Aperiodic parameters could provide a stable individual baseline against which changes, for example after a treatment change or before a seizure, are more easily detected, whereas alpha-based measures may better capture the current functional state, in line with their sensitivity to medication (see 4.4).
The overall correlation structure among measures was largely preserved between epilepsy and controls.
This indicates that these candidate proxies, while capturing distinct aspects of neural dynamics, maintain a broadly similar pattern of interrelationships across groups 13 .
text.formatted: This indicates that these candidate proxies, while capturing distinct aspects of neural dynamics, maintain a broadly similar pattern of interrelationships across groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> .

text.text: In other words, epilepsy does not fundamentally rewire the way these measures co-vary; rather, it appears to displace the network along a shared axis of excitability without generating a qualitatively different pattern of interdependencies.
All the measures tested here were selected as they are believed to reflect the excitation-inhibition balance, and as such one would expect them to co-vary, or at least vary in the same direction.
Yet, they often diverged.
No single metric fully captures cortical excitability.
Rather, different measures appear to reflect complementary dimensions of neural dynamics, suggesting to not treat any one of them as a stand-alone index of E/I balance.
The most consistent medication finding was that, within the same person, sessions with one additional ASM showed higher relative alpha power.
We interpret this as a signature of the shift toward inhibition that ASMs are designed to produce.

Most ASMs, through enhanced GABAergic transmission, reduced glutamatergic transmission or modulation of voltage-gated channels, reduce network excitability 6 , and alpha-band activity is considered a correlate of cortical inhibition and of the thalamocortical gating of cortical activity 55 .
text.formatted: Most ASMs, through enhanced GABAergic transmission, reduced glutamatergic transmission or modulation of voltage-gated channels, reduce network excitability <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> , and alpha-band activity is considered a correlate of cortical inhibition and of the thalamocortical gating of cortical activity <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">55</ref> .

text.text: A higher relative alpha with more drugs is therefore in the direction expected if medication increases inhibitory tone and stabilizes cortical dynamics.
The fact that the effect was seen in relative rather than absolute alpha suggests a redistribution of spectral power toward the alpha band, and not simply a global change in amplitude.
The within-person design strengthens this interpretation, since each patient serves as their own control and stable differences in epilepsy type, etiology and severity are removed.
The between-person comparison did not show this association, and this is also informative.
Patients receiving more drugs generally have more severe or refractory epilepsy, whose EEG may differ from that of milder cases in the opposite direction.

The disease-related and drug-related contributions to alpha power may therefore partly offset each other when patients are compared with one another, but become visible when each patient is compared with themselves.
Finally, changes in ASM count were not associated with changes in within-session or across-session variability.
A reasonable interpretation is that medication shifts the level of these measures without altering how reproducible they are, so that each patient retains a characteristic profile under treatment.
This is consistent with the idea that the stable aperiodic signature persists across treatment changes.

Because exposure was a coarse count that pooled drugs with different mechanisms, and because changes in treatment follow clinical course, these associations should be seen as pointing to a general shift toward inhibition and not as drug-specific effects.
More granular data (e.g., daily dosage) would allow a mechanistic test of this account.
These results do not support using any of the evaluated measures as a stand-alone diagnostic biomarker.
The aperiodic parameters were the most promising candidates, and their detectability in routine, heterogeneous clinical EEG is encouraging.
The offset and exponent are better viewed as candidates for further validation, for example in prospective cohorts with defined epilepsy types, drug-naïve patients and standardized acquisition.
Our findings on relative alpha power suggest that medication status should be recorded and modelled whenever such measures are considered for treatment monitoring.
Several limitations should be acknowledged.
First, the use of routine clinical EEG introduces variability in recording conditions, electrode configurations, and patient state, all of which may influence the measured signals.
Although this heterogeneity enhances generalizability, it may also reduce sensitivity to subtle effects.
Second, our analysis adopted a global, wholebrain approach and therefore does not account for spatial heterogeneity or focal epileptogenic regions.
This limitation was intrinsically related to the available data.
In fact, TUEP dataset does not contain ready to use information regarding the epilepsy type (e.g., focal vs generalized), nor location distinction in case of focal epilepsy.
This prevents inference on the significance of potential electrode based analysis.
Third, ASM burden was quantified as the number of medications rather than dosage or pharmacological class, limiting the precision of medication-related analyses.
Finally, the observational nature of the dataset precludes causal inference regarding the relationships among excitability measures, epilepsy, and treatment.
Future work should aim to integrate spatially resolved measures, incorporate more detailed pharmacological information, and validate these findings in prospective, standardized datasets.
Combining EEG-derived metrics with other modalities, such as structural or functional neuroimaging, may further improve characterization of epileptic networks.

In addition, the development of composite indices of excitability, potentially informed by machine learning approaches, represents a promising avenue for translating these findings into clinically actionable tools.
In summary, this study provides a comprehensive evaluation of EEG-derived proxies of cortical excitability in epilepsy.
Our findings highlight the robustness of aperiodic spectral parameters, and the influence of ASM treatment on electrophysiological signatures.

These findings support aperiodic parameters as candidates for further investigation, and they show that multiple, complementary measures and careful accounting for medication are needed in studies of EEG-based excitability markers.
Our results also confirm that quantitative analysis of excitability markers extracted from routing recordings carry relevant information on epilepsy.
